::: {.callout-note}
**This syllabus is the contract between the course and the student.** It lists every
topic, the order it is taught in, the dataset it is taught on, and what the student
can do afterwards.

**It is a reorganisation of the 16-session draft, not a replacement.** Every topic in
the draft survives; the sequence, the grouping and the depth have changed.
[Appendix B](#sec-coverage) maps every draft bullet to its new home, and
[Appendix A](#sec-review) explains each change. Topics marked ➕ are additions.
:::

## What changed, in one screen {#sec-changes}

| # | Change | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Statistics and EDA moved before cleaning** (draft S7–S8 → new S4–S5) | You cannot call a value an outlier before you know the distribution. The draft removed outliers in S3 and taught the IQR in S7. |
| 2 | **The train–test split moved before scaling** (new S7) | The draft scaled data in S5 and first split it in S9. Every student who followed that order leaked test data into training. |
| 3 | **A Python and NumPy session added** (new S2) | The draft opened Pandas in S2 with no Python and no NumPy behind it. |
| 4 | **A classification session added** (new S10) | The draft taught regression only, then asked for "advanced machine learning models" in the capstone. |
| 5 | **Model evaluation moved ahead of clustering** (draft S11 → new S11) | Cross-validation and over/underfitting are the vocabulary the clustering session needs to justify a choice of *k*. |
| 6 | **Association rule mining taught, not just assigned** (new S12) | The draft required it in the capstone and never covered it. |
| 7 | **Data integration merged into the Pandas session** (draft S4 → new S3) | A five-item taxonomy plus one `.merge()` demo is not a session; joining data is what Pandas is for. |
| 8 | **The three big-data sessions became two, plus a runnable path** (draft S13–S15 → new S14–S15) | Hadoop and MapReduce belong together; HDFS-on-a-laptop needs an execution plan, which the draft did not give. |

Session count is unchanged at 16.

## Course description {#sec-description}

Data science turns recorded facts into decisions. This course walks that path once,
end to end, and then walks it again at a scale where the data no longer fits in
memory.

The student starts with a raw, dirty CSV and finishes with a model that other people
can use through a web page, plus the judgement to say when its answer should not be
trusted. Along the way they learn the statistics that make a chart honest, the
preprocessing order that keeps a result real, and the distributed tools that apply
when a single machine is not enough.

**The course is practical.** Every session has a live demo and a hands-on lab, and
every technique is taught on a named dataset that actually contains the problem the
technique solves.

## Who this course is for {#sec-audience}

Students and early-career professionals who want to work with data as engineers,
analysts or scientists — including those with no machine learning background.

**Assumed:** comfort with a computer, school-level algebra, willingness to read an
error message.

**Not assumed:** Python, statistics, machine learning, or any prior tooling. Session 2
starts from variables.

::: {.callout-tip title="➕ Pre-work for students who have never written code"}
Three self-paced notebooks, to be finished before Session 2. They start at
`print()`:

- [Python foundations A](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/blob/main/mlai-genai-internship/student/notebooks/00a_python_foundations.ipynb) — printing, variables, types, operators, strings
- [Python foundations B](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/blob/main/mlai-genai-internship/student/notebooks/00b_python_foundations_2.ipynb) — collections, conditions, loops, functions
- [Python scenarios](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/blob/main/mlai-genai-internship/student/notebooks/00c_python_scenarios.ipynb) — ten real problems; **Scenario 10 cleans a messy dataset by hand**, which is exactly what Sessions 6–7 then do with Pandas

Students who have done Scenario 10 understand *why* the preprocessing steps exist.
Students who have not copy six lines and learn nothing.
:::

## Course learning outcomes {#sec-outcomes}

By the end of the course a student can:

1. **Frame** a business question as a data science problem with a measurable target.
2. **Acquire and integrate** data from files, databases, APIs and the web into one
   analysable table.
3. **Describe** a dataset numerically — centre, spread, shape — and say what the
   numbers rule out.
4. **Explore** a dataset visually and defend which chart answers which question.
5. **Clean and prepare** data in an order that does not leak information from the test
   set into the model.
6. **Build, compare and tune** regression, classification and clustering models with
   scikit-learn.
7. **Evaluate** a model honestly — the right metric, cross-validated, with residual
   and error analysis.
8. **Deploy** a trained model as a Streamlit application that another person can use.
9. **Process** data too large for one machine with Hadoop, MapReduce and Spark, and
   store it in a NoSQL database.
10. **Deliver** an end-to-end project with reproducible code, honest reporting of what
    did not work, and a stated view on bias and privacy.

## How the course is organised {#sec-organisation}

Five parts. They are an argument, not a list: **you cannot prepare data you have not
described; you cannot model data you have not prepared; you cannot deploy a model you
have not evaluated; and none of it changes when the data gets large — only the
machinery does.**

| Part | Sessions | Question it answers | Shape |
|---|---|---|---|
| [**A — Foundations**](#sec-part-a) | 1–3 | *What is this field, and how do I touch data at all?* | Concept drill |
| [**B — Understanding the data**](#sec-part-b) | 4–5 | *What is actually in this file?* | Concept drill |
| [**C — Preparing the data**](#sec-part-c) | 6–8 | *How do I make it fit to model without cheating?* | Applied walkthrough |
| [**D — Modelling and evaluation**](#sec-part-d) | 9–12 | *What can be learned from it, and is the answer real?* | Applied walkthrough |
| [**E — Delivery and scale**](#sec-part-e) | 13–16 | *How do others use it, and what if it does not fit in memory?* | Applied walkthrough |

::: {.callout-note title="How to read a session entry"}
**Topics** are what is taught. A ➕ marks a topic added to the draft.

# Part A — Foundations {#sec-part-a}

*Three sessions to answer one question: what is this field, and what do I type to
touch a dataset at all?*

### Session 1 — Introduction to Data Science and the Analytics Lifecycle {#sec-s01}

*Sets the map the other fifteen sessions are drawn on.*

**Topics**

- Introduction to Data Science — definition, and what separates it from reporting
- Evolution of Data Science — statistics → business intelligence → big data → machine
  learning → generative AI
- Data Science roles — data analyst, data engineer, data scientist, ML engineer,
  BI developer; who owns which lifecycle stage
- Applications of data science across sectors — healthcare, finance, retail,
  logistics, agriculture, public services
- ➕ Data Science vs Statistics vs Machine Learning vs AI vs Generative AI — the
  nested picture, and the honest boundaries between them
- ➕ Types of data: **structured** (tables, CSV, SQL), **semi-structured** (JSON, XML,
  logs), **unstructured** (text, image, audio, video) — with what each costs to work
  with
- ➕ The data science lifecycle: problem definition → data collection → cleaning and
  preprocessing → exploration → feature engineering → modelling → evaluation →
  deployment → monitoring
- ➕ The toolchain: Python, Jupyter, Google Colab, conda, Git, and where each fits
- ➕ Where the data comes from: open dataset repositories (Kaggle, UCI, data.gov,
  Hugging Face Datasets) and how to read a dataset licence
- ➕ Responsible data science, previewed: consent, bias, privacy, reproducibility —
  returned to in [Session 16](#sec-s16)

**Demo** — An interactive, real-world data science dashboard (a live weather or stock
predictor), traced backwards through the lifecycle: *this chart came from this model,
which came from this table, which came from these three sources.*

**Lab** — ➕ Environment check. Every student installs the `ds` environment, runs
`check_setup.py`, opens Colab, and prints the version of every library the course
uses. A student who cannot do this today cannot do Session 2.

**Dataset** — None. Concepts only.

**By the end** — The student can name the seven lifecycle stages in order, place each
job role against the stages it owns, and classify a given data source as structured,
semi-structured or unstructured.

### Session 2 — ➕ Python and NumPy Essentials for Data Science {#sec-s02}

*Added session. The draft opened Pandas in Session 2 with nothing underneath it.*

**Topics**

- ➕ Python refresher: variables, data types, operators, conditional statements,
  loops, functions
- ➕ Collections: list, tuple, dictionary, set — and which one a data problem wants
- ➕ Strings and formatting; reading and writing files
- ➕ Classes and objects, briefly — enough to read `model.fit()` and know what `model`
  is
- ➕ Why libraries exist: the cost of a Python loop over a million numbers
- ➕ NumPy: creating arrays, array indexing, array slicing, data types, copy vs view,
  array shape, reshape, iterating
- ➕ Vectorised arithmetic and broadcasting
- ➕ Aggregations and axis-wise statistics; boolean masking and `where`
- ➕ Random numbers and **seeding** — every result in this course is reproducible

**Demo** — The same calculation twice: a Python `for` loop over one million values,
then one NumPy expression. Time both. The number on screen is the argument for the
rest of the course.

**Lab** — ➕ The marks calculator: load exam scores into an array, compute per-student
and per-subject means, flag every score below one standard deviation from the mean
using a boolean mask, without writing a loop.

**Dataset** — Generated arrays, seeded.

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Copy versus view"}
`b = a[2:5]` does not copy — writing to `b` changes `a`. This is the single most
common source of "my data changed and I did not change it" in the whole course, and
it is taught here so it never has to be debugged later.
:::

**By the end** — The student can write a function, index and reshape an array, and
replace a loop with a vectorised expression.

### Session 3 — Data Collection, Integration and Pandas Fundamentals {#sec-s03}

*Merges draft Session 2 and draft Session 4. Getting data in, and putting it
together, are one job.*

**Topics**

*Collecting*

- Data collection strategies — primary vs secondary, surveys, sensors and IoT,
  transactional systems, public datasets, web scraping, third-party APIs
- ➕ Sampling: random, stratified, systematic, convenience — and the bias each one
  introduces
- ➕ Legal and ethical collection: robots.txt, terms of service, personal data
- Data pre-processing overview — the roadmap of Part C, shown once here so the
  student knows what is coming and why

*Handling with Pandas*

- Working with Pandas DataFrames — Series vs DataFrame, index, dtypes
- ➕ Reading from four sources: `read_csv`, `read_excel`, `read_json`, `read_sql`, and
  a REST API response
- ➕ Inspecting: `.head()`, `.info()`, `.describe()`, `.shape`, `.dtypes`,
  `.value_counts()`
- ➕ Selecting and filtering: `[]`, `.loc`, `.iloc`, boolean masks
- ➕ Reshaping and summarising: `groupby`, `agg`, `sort_values`, `apply`, `pivot`
- ➕ Writing results back out: `to_csv`, `to_excel`

*Integrating*

- Data integration approaches — **virtual integration** (query many sources as one,
  nothing is copied), **physical data integration** (copy everything into a
  warehouse), **application-based integration** (each application does its own
  translating), **manual integration** (a human copies and pastes), **middleware
  data integration** (a layer in between does the translating)
- ➕ Which approach a given situation calls for, as a comparison table: freshness,
  cost, failure mode
- ➕ Combining tables in Pandas: `concat`, `merge`, `join`
- ➕ Join types — inner, left, right, outer — and the row count that proves which one
  happened
- ➕ Integration problems the taxonomy hides: schema conflicts, duplicate entities
  under different spellings, unit mismatches, redundant columns

**Demo** — Loading a raw, messy CSV into a Pandas DataFrame and running `.head()`,
`.info()` and `.describe()` to inspect the raw structure. Then `.merge()` and
`.join()` to combine a *Customer Info* table with a *Purchase History* table on a
common ID — and, deliberately, the same merge done wrong, so the class watches the
row count explode from 500 to 4,300.

**Lab** — Load three files (CSV, Excel, JSON), reconcile their differing column names
and ID formats, join them into one table, and report the row count after each step.

**Dataset** — [`prepreprocessing/pre_data.csv`](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/blob/main/datasets/prepreprocessing/pre_data.csv)
(12 rows, small enough to check by eye) and
[`regression/cardekho_dataset.csv`](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/blob/main/datasets/regression/cardekho_dataset.csv)
(real, and messy). Customer/purchase tables are generated by a committed, seeded
script, `datasets/make_customers.py`.

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Check the row count after every join"}
A merge that silently multiplies rows is the most expensive undetected error in this
course: everything downstream still runs, the model trains, the accuracy looks fine,
and the result is meaningless. **Print `len(df)` before and after. Every time.**
:::

**By the end** — The student can load data from four source types, join tables with
the correct join type, and detect a bad join from the row count alone.

# Part B — Understanding the data {#sec-part-b}

*Two sessions, moved ahead of cleaning. Nothing in Part C can be decided without
them: an outlier is only extreme relative to a distribution you have already
measured.*

### Session 4 — Descriptive Statistics for Data Science {#sec-s04}

*Was draft Session 7. Moved forward by three sessions.*

**Topics**

- Measures of central tendency and dispersion — the two questions every column
  answers first
- Mean, median, mode; standard deviation, variance, range — and **which average to
  report when the data is skewed**
- ➕ Percentiles, quartiles, the interquartile range and the five-number summary —
  the machinery [Session 6](#sec-s06) uses to detect outliers
- ➕ Z-scores and standardised comparison across different units
- Skewness and kurtosis — what a shape number means before you have seen the picture
- Frequency distributions, histograms and bin width; the effect of choosing bins
  badly
- ➕ Probability distributions in brief: uniform, normal, binomial, Poisson — and how
  to tell whether your column is plausibly normal
- ➕ Populations, samples, sampling error and the standard error of the mean
- ➕ Inferential essentials: confidence intervals, the null hypothesis, the p-value,
  the *t*-test, the chi-square test of independence, one-way ANOVA
- ➕ What a p-value does **not** mean, stated explicitly

**Demo** — Summary statistics on a real dataset, then a histogram with a normal curve
overlaid, so skewness and kurtosis stop being numbers and become a shape. Then the
same column's mean and median side by side, with the gap between them explained.

**Lab** — Profile every numeric column of the car dataset: report centre, spread and
shape for each, then answer one question with a *t*-test — *do diesel and petrol cars
differ in selling price, or is the gap sampling noise?*

**Dataset** — [`regression/cardekho_dataset.csv`](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/blob/main/datasets/regression/cardekho_dataset.csv)
(strongly skewed prices — the mean and median disagree, which is the point) and
[`classification/heart_failure_raw.csv`](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/blob/main/datasets/classification/heart_failure_raw.csv).

::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Analogy — centre and spread"}
Reporting the mean without the standard deviation is like describing a journey by its
average speed and nothing else. *Average 60 km/h* is true of a steady cruise and of an
hour of stop-start traffic. **The spread is the part that tells you what the trip was
actually like.**
:::

**By the end** — The student can report centre, spread and shape for any column,
choose mean or median with a stated reason, and interpret a p-value correctly in one
sentence.

### Session 5 — Exploratory Data Analysis and Visualization {#sec-s05}

*Was draft Session 8. Also absorbs "statistical methods for visualization" from draft
Session 15, which belongs with the charts, not with the databases.*

**Topics**

- Basic plots using Matplotlib — figure and axes, line, bar, histogram, scatter,
  labels, titles, saving
- ➕ Seaborn for statistical graphics — `countplot`, `histplot`, `boxplot`,
  `violinplot`, `pairplot`, `heatmap`
- Box plots — the five-number summary drawn, and the whisker rule that defines an
  outlier
- Pivot tables — cross-tabulating two categoricals against a numeric summary
- Correlation statistics and the correlation coefficient — Pearson, and ➕ Spearman
  for ranks
- Correlation and scatter plots — reading strength, direction and non-linearity off a
  picture
- ➕ The EDA framework: univariate → bivariate → multivariate, and the five questions
  to ask of any new dataset
- ➕ Statistical methods for visualization: distribution plots, density estimates,
  error bars and confidence bands, aggregation before plotting — the honest way to
  draw a summary
- ➕ Visualising missingness: a null-matrix heatmap that shows whether gaps are random
  or structured
- ➕ Choosing the chart: a chart-chooser table mapping *question type* → *chart*
- ➕ Correlation is not causation; confounders; Simpson's paradox with a worked
  two-group example

**Demo** — A dynamic visual report: a Seaborn correlation heatmap plus a scatter
matrix, used to identify which variables are most heavily correlated — followed by
the trap, where the strongest correlation in the matrix turns out to be two columns
measuring the same thing in different units.

**Lab** — ➕ *Data detective*, in pairs. Each pair gets a dataset and thirty minutes to
answer five questions with five charts, then presents the one chart that surprised
them.

**Dataset** — [`regression/cardekho_dataset.csv`](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/blob/main/datasets/regression/cardekho_dataset.csv)
and [`loan_data_10k.csv`](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/blob/main/datasets/loan_data_10k.csv).

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ A chart is a question, not decoration"}
Every chart in this course must be introduced by the question it answers. A chart with
no question attached is where fabricated conclusions come from — the eye finds a
pattern in anything.
:::

**By the end** — The student can pick the chart that answers a stated question, read a
correlation heatmap, and give one concrete example where a strong correlation is not
a cause.

# Part C — Preparing the data {#sec-part-c}

*Three sessions taught in a fixed order. The order is the lesson: run these steps in a
different sequence and you will get a number that looks fine and is wrong.*

::: {.callout-important title="🔓 The preprocessing sequence — used in every session from here on"}
```text
1 LOAD → 2 EXPLORE → 3 DUPLICATES → 4 IMPOSSIBLE VALUES → 5 MISSING VALUES
→ 6 OUTLIERS → 7 ENCODING → 8 TRAIN–TEST SPLIT → 9 SCALING
```

Two of these positions are not negotiable:

- **Impossible values before missing values.** An age of 160 is an error, not an
  extreme. Turn it into `NaN` first and let imputation deal with it; do it the other
  way round and the error is imputed *into* your data.
- **Scaling after the split, fitted on train only.** The same holds for imputation,
  encoding, feature selection and PCA. Anything that learns from the data goes inside
  a `Pipeline`.
:::

### Session 6 — Data Cleaning {#sec-s06}

*Was draft Session 3. Moved after statistics and EDA, because steps 3–6 of the
sequence above all need numbers the student now has.*

**Topics**

- ➕ Duplicates: exact and near-duplicate rows, `duplicated()`, `drop_duplicates()`,
  and choosing which copy to keep
- ➕ Impossible values: negative ages, future dates, zero-valued blood pressure —
  finding them with domain rules, converting them to `NaN`
- Filling missing values — mean, median and mode imputation; forward and backward
  fill; ➕ group-wise imputation; ➕ KNN imputation; ➕ when to drop instead of fill
- ➕ Types of missingness (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) and why an imputed column needs a
  `was_missing` flag
- Smoothing noisy data — ➕ binning (equal-width and equal-frequency means),
  regression smoothing, rolling averages, and clustering-based smoothing
- Detecting and removing outliers — the IQR rule, the z-score rule, ➕ visual
  detection by box plot and scatter
- ➕ Handling, not just removing: capping and winsorising, transforming, or keeping
  the outlier because it is the signal
- ➕ Structural cleaning: wrong data types, inconsistent date formats, stray
  whitespace, mixed category spellings
- ➕ Reporting: what the cleaning pass found, as a table, in the notebook

**Demo** — Programmatically replacing `NaN` values with column means, and plotting a
box plot before and after filtering extreme outliers. Then the counter-demo: the same
filter applied to fraud data, which deletes every fraud case in the file.

**Lab** — Run the full nine-step sequence on the heart-failure dataset and produce a
one-page cleaning report: rows in, duplicates removed, impossible values found,
values imputed and by what rule, outliers found and what was done with them, rows out.

**Dataset** — [`prepreprocessing/pre_data.csv`](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/blob/main/datasets/prepreprocessing/pre_data.csv)
first, cleaned **by hand** on paper — twelve rows, every problem visible — then
[`classification/heart_failure_raw.csv`](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/blob/main/datasets/classification/heart_failure_raw.csv)
in code.

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ An outlier is not automatically an error"}
In a fraud dataset the outliers *are* the fraud. In a sensor dataset they are usually
a fault. **The dataset does not tell you which; the domain does.** Never delete a row
on a rule alone — look at it first.
:::

**By the end** — The student can execute the nine-step sequence in order, justify each
imputation choice, and give one case where removing outliers destroys the analysis.

### Session 7 — Data Transformation, Encoding and the Train–Test Split {#sec-s07}

*Was draft Session 5. Extended with encoding and the split, because scaling without
them was the draft's most serious ordering fault.*

**Topics**

- Rescaling data — `MinMaxScaler` to a fixed range
- Standardizing data — `StandardScaler` to mean 0, standard deviation 1
- Normalizing data — `Normalizer` on rows to unit norm, and why this is a different
  operation from the other two despite the name
- Binarizing data — `Binarizer` and thresholding a continuous column
- ➕ `RobustScaler`, for data that still contains outliers you chose to keep
- ➕ Which scaler which algorithm needs: distance-based and gradient-based models care;
  tree-based models do not
- ➕ Non-linear transforms: log, square-root, Box-Cox and Yeo-Johnson for skewed
  columns
- ➕ Encoding categorical data: `LabelEncoder` for the target, one-hot / dummy
  variables for nominal features, ordinal encoding for ordered categories
- ➕ The dummy variable trap, and high-cardinality columns that one-hot encoding
  cannot handle
- ➕ **The train–test split**: `train_test_split`, `test_size`, `random_state`,
  `stratify` — with the course-wide naming convention `X_train, X_test, y_train,
  y_test`
- ➕ **Data leakage** — the single most common serious mistake in student projects —
  and the three forms it takes: scaling before splitting, imputing before splitting,
  and features that encode the answer
- ➕ `Pipeline` and `ColumnTransformer`: making the correct order structural instead
  of remembered

**Demo** — `MinMaxScaler` and `StandardScaler` applied to a dataset, with the
distribution plotted before and after so the class sees the shape hold and the axis
move. Then the leakage demo: the same model scored twice, once scaled before the
split and once after, with both numbers on screen and the gap named.

**Lab** — Take the cleaned dataset from Session 6 and build one `Pipeline` that
imputes, encodes and scales, fitted on the training split only. Prove it is correct by
showing the test set was never touched during `fit`.

**Dataset** — [`loan_data_10k.csv`](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/blob/main/datasets/loan_data_10k.csv)
— mixed numeric and categorical, columns on very different scales, an imbalanced
target that makes `stratify` matter.

::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Analogy — studying with the answer key"}
Fitting a scaler on all the data before splitting is revising for an exam using the
marked answer paper. You will score brilliantly in practice and badly on the day.
**The test set must be data the pipeline has never seen — not even its mean.**
:::

**By the end** — The student can split before transforming, choose a scaler with a
stated reason, encode both nominal and ordinal categoricals, and name three ways
leakage gets in.

### Session 8 — Data Reduction, Discretization and Feature Engineering {#sec-s08}

*Was draft Session 6. Placed after transformation because PCA needs standardised
inputs, which the draft had not yet introduced when it taught PCA.*

**Topics**

*Reduction*

- Dimensionality reduction — why 200 columns is often worse than 20; the curse of
  dimensionality
- ➕ Feature selection before projection: **filter** methods (variance threshold,
  correlation, chi-square, mutual information), **wrapper** methods (recursive feature
  elimination), **embedded** methods (Lasso, tree feature importance)
- ➕ Projection methods: **PCA**, and briefly **LDA** and **t-SNE** — what each is for
  and why t-SNE is for looking, not for modelling
- ➕ Explained variance ratio and the scree plot — choosing how many components to
  keep
- ➕ The cost of PCA: components are combinations, so interpretability is gone
- Data cube aggregation — rolling detail up along dimensions (day → month → year);
  the OLAP idea, and its Pandas equivalent in `groupby` and `pivot_table`
- Numerosity reduction — replacing the data with something smaller: ➕ parametric
  (a fitted model or regression stands in for the rows) and non-parametric
  (sampling, histograms, clustering)

*Discretization*

- Top-down discretization (splitting) — start with the whole range and cut it:
  equal-width binning, entropy-based splits
- Bottom-up discretization (merging) — start with every distinct value and merge
  neighbours: chi-merge
- ➕ `pd.cut` for equal-width and `pd.qcut` for equal-frequency bins; choosing cut
  points from domain knowledge rather than from convenience
- ➕ What binning costs: information thrown away in exchange for robustness and
  readability

*Feature engineering*

- ➕ Creating features: ratios, differences, date parts (year, month, weekday, age),
  text length, interaction terms, domain-specific ratios
- ➕ Feature engineering worked on two real datasets — used-car and heart-failure
- ➕ Data augmentation: what it is, when it is used, and the tabular, image and text
  techniques — including which augmentations are legitimate and which change the label

**Demo** — PCA compressing a dataset from 10 features to 2, with the explained
variance printed so the compression has a cost attached; and `pd.cut` discretizing
continuous age into "Teen", "Adult", "Senior".

**Lab** — Reduce a 30-column dataset to 6 columns three ways — filter selection,
embedded selection, PCA — and compare the model score for each against the full set.

**Dataset** — [`classification/diabetes_prediction_dataset.csv`](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/blob/main/datasets/classification/diabetes_prediction_dataset.csv)
and [`classification/adult.csv`](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/blob/main/datasets/classification/adult.csv)
(high-cardinality categoricals, dates, mixed types).

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Measure the reduction, do not assume it"}
Engineered features and dimensionality reduction do not reliably improve a model. On
real course data, hand-built features have moved linear R² by **+0.0001** and made a
random forest **worse**. Report the number you actually get, including when it
contradicts the lesson.
:::

**By the end** — The student can select features three different ways, choose the
number of PCA components from a scree plot, and state what binning cost them.

# Part D — Modelling and evaluation {#sec-part-d}

*Four sessions. Regression and classification give the student two model families;
evaluation then decides whether either of them is real; clustering closes the part by
applying the same discipline where there is no answer key at all.*

### Session 9 — Supervised Learning I: Regression {#sec-s09}

*Was draft Session 9, unchanged in position, extended with the metrics it needs.*

**Topics**

- Supervised learning techniques — the labelled-data idea; regression vs
  classification as *number* vs *category*
- Prediction and decision making — the gap between a predicted value and an action
  taken because of it
- Simple linear regression — one feature, the line of best fit, slope and intercept
  read as sentences
- Multiple regression — several features, and what a coefficient means when the other
  columns are held constant
- ➕ The scikit-learn API in four calls: `fit`, `predict`, `score`, `transform` — the
  shape of every model in the rest of the course
- ➕ Regression metrics: MAE, MSE, RMSE, R², adjusted R² — which one to report and to
  whom
- ➕ Assumptions of linear regression: linearity, independence, homoscedasticity,
  normal residuals, no severe multicollinearity (VIF)
- ➕ Polynomial regression, and the point where flexibility becomes overfitting
- ➕ Regularization in brief: Ridge and Lasso, and what the penalty buys

**Demo** — Training a multiple linear regression with scikit-learn to predict real
estate prices from inputs such as floor area and number of bedrooms, then reading the
coefficients out loud as sentences: *"each extra bedroom is worth ₹X, holding area
constant"* — including the coefficient whose sign is the wrong way round, and why.

**Lab** — Predict used-car selling price. Start with one feature, add features one at
a time, and record R² and RMSE at every step in a table. Stop when adding a feature
stops helping, and say why it stopped.

**Dataset** — [`regression/salary_data.csv`](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/blob/main/datasets/regression/salary_data.csv)
(one feature, one line — the smallest honest example), then
[`regression/cardekho_dataset.csv`](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/blob/main/datasets/regression/cardekho_dataset.csv).
The demo uses the California housing dataset that ships with scikit-learn, so it needs
no download.

**By the end** — The student can fit and interpret a multiple regression, report the
right error metric for an audience, and check two regression assumptions.

### Session 10 — ➕ Supervised Learning II: Classification {#sec-s10}

*Added session. The draft never taught classification, then required "advanced machine
learning models" in the capstone.*

**Topics**

- ➕ The classification problem: binary, multiclass, multilabel
- ➕ Logistic regression — the linear model bent into a probability; the decision
  threshold as a separate, tunable choice
- ➕ k-Nearest Neighbours — the algorithm that does no training, and why it needs
  scaled features
- ➕ Decision trees — splits, impurity, depth, and why a tree is readable
- ➕ Random forests — many trees, voting, and feature importance
- ➕ Naive Bayes and Support Vector Machines, briefly, with the situation each suits
- ➕ The confusion matrix — true and false positives and negatives, drawn once and
  used everywhere
- ➕ Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, specificity — and the cost of the mistake that
  decides which one matters
- ➕ ROC curves, AUC, and the precision–recall curve for imbalanced data
- ➕ Class imbalance: `stratify`, class weights, resampling, SMOTE
- ➕ Predicting probabilities rather than labels, and choosing the threshold from the
  business cost

**Demo** — Logistic regression and a random forest on the loan dataset, side by side.
Then the useless 99% model: a classifier that predicts "no default" for everyone,
scores 99% accuracy, and catches zero defaulters. The confusion matrix is the only
thing on screen that shows it.

**Lab** — Build a loan-approval classifier. Report the confusion matrix, choose
between precision and recall with a written justification about what a wrong decision
costs the bank and the applicant, then move the threshold to match that choice.

**Dataset** — [`loan_data_10k.csv`](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/blob/main/datasets/loan_data_10k.csv)
(imbalanced, so accuracy is visibly the wrong metric) and
[`classification/iris.csv`](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/blob/main/datasets/classification/iris.csv)
for the multiclass case.

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Accuracy is the default metric and it is usually the wrong one"}
On data where 99 of 100 rows share a label, a model that has learned nothing scores
99%. **Report the confusion matrix before you report accuracy, every time.**
:::

**By the end** — The student can train four classifiers, read a confusion matrix, and
choose a metric from the cost of the error rather than from habit.

### Session 11 — Model Evaluation, Validation and Tuning {#sec-s11}

*Was draft Session 11. Moved ahead of clustering, because the next session's choice of
*k* has to be defended, and this is where the vocabulary for defending a choice is
taught.*

**Topics**

- Model evaluation techniques — ➕ holdout validation, k-fold cross-validation,
  stratified k-fold, leave-one-out, bootstrapping; the trade-off between them
- ➕ Overfitting and underfitting — bias and variance, seen as two failure pictures
  rather than two definitions
- ➕ Learning curves and validation curves — telling "needs more data" apart from
  "needs a different model"
- Model evaluation using visualization — ➕ predicted-vs-actual plots, error
  distributions, confusion-matrix heatmaps, ROC overlays for competing models
- Residual plots and distributional plots — checking residuals are random,
  homoscedastic and roughly normal, and reading the three failure shapes
- ➕ Hyperparameter tuning: `GridSearchCV`, `RandomizedSearchCV`, and Bayesian
  optimization in concept
- ➕ Nested cross-validation, and why tuning on the test set silently invalidates the
  score
- ➕ Baselines: `DummyRegressor` and `DummyClassifier`. **A model that cannot beat the
  baseline has not worked, whatever its R².**
- ➕ Error analysis: looking at the rows the model got wrong, not just the score
- ➕ Data leakage, revisited — the leaked column that makes a bad model look excellent

**Demo** — Plotting the residuals of the Session 9 regression to check visually for
random distribution and homoscedasticity, plus predicted versus actual. Then the same
model cross-validated five ways, with five different scores printed — so "the
accuracy" stops being a single number.

**Lab** — Take one model from Session 9 and one from Session 10. Cross-validate both,
tune both with a grid search, plot the learning curve for each, and write three
sentences on what the curve says to do next.

**Dataset** — The models and splits from Sessions 9 and 10, reused deliberately.

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ One split is one opinion"}
Change `random_state` and the score changes. If a decision between two models depends
on a difference smaller than the spread across folds, **the decision has not been
made** — it has been guessed.
:::

**By the end** — The student can cross-validate a model, read a learning curve,
tune hyperparameters without touching the test set, and beat a stated baseline.

### Session 12 — Unsupervised Learning: Clustering and Association Rules {#sec-s12}

*Was draft Session 10, extended with the association rule mining the draft required in
the capstone but never taught.*

**Topics**

*Clustering*

- Unsupervised learning techniques — learning structure with no labels; clustering,
  dimensionality reduction and association rules as its three families
- Introduction to clustering — what a cluster is, and the fact that there is no
  correct answer to check against
- K-Means clustering — centroids, assignment and update steps, convergence,
  `random_state` and `n_init`
- ➕ Choosing *k*: the elbow method on inertia, and the silhouette score — with the
  case where the two disagree
- ➕ **Scale before you cluster.** K-Means measures distance, so an unscaled income
  column decides every cluster on its own
- ➕ Hierarchical clustering — agglomerative linkage and reading a dendrogram
- ➕ DBSCAN — density-based clusters of arbitrary shape, and explicit noise points
- ➕ Cluster profiling: describing each segment in business language, which is the
  actual deliverable

*Association rule mining*

- ➕ Market basket analysis — transactions, itemsets, and the question *"what is
  bought together?"*
- ➕ Support, confidence and lift, computed by hand on a ten-transaction table before
  any library is imported
- ➕ The Apriori algorithm and the downward-closure property; FP-Growth in brief
- ➕ `mlxtend` for `apriori` and `association_rules`
- ➕ Reading a rule critically: high confidence with a lift of 1.0 means the rule
  discovered nothing

**Demo** — K-Means on a mall customer dataset, grouping shoppers by income and
spending score, shown as a colour-coded 2D scatter with the centroids marked. Then the
same run without scaling, so the class sees the clusters change completely.

**Lab** — Segment the mall customers, choose *k* with both an elbow plot and a
silhouette curve, and write a one-paragraph description of each segment a marketing
team could act on. Then mine a grocery basket file for rules with lift above 1.2 and
say which one is actually useful.

**Dataset** — [`clustering/Mall_Customers.csv`](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/blob/main/datasets/clustering/Mall_Customers.csv);
basket transactions generated by a committed, seeded script, `datasets/make_baskets.py`,
which plants three known rules so the student can check the algorithm found them.

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Clustering always returns clusters"}
Ask K-Means for four groups in pure random noise and it will give you four groups,
each with a centroid and a colour. **The silhouette score is the check** — and on real
course data it has preferred the wrong clustering, so it is a check, not a verdict.
:::

**By the end** — The student can scale, cluster, choose *k* with two methods, describe
each cluster in business terms, and compute support, confidence and lift by hand.

# Part E — Delivery and scale {#sec-part-e}

*Four sessions. A model nobody can use has not been delivered, and a method that only
works on data that fits in memory has not scaled. This part fixes both, then the
capstone puts the whole course into one project.*

### Session 13 — Model Saving and Deployment with Streamlit {#sec-s13}

*Was draft Session 12, unchanged in position.*

**Topics**

- Saving trained models — `joblib` and `pickle`, ➕ what is actually inside the file,
  and why the **whole pipeline** must be saved rather than the estimator alone
- ➕ Loading and inference: a single `predict_one()` function that takes raw user input
  and returns a prediction, used identically by the notebook and the app
- ➕ Model versioning and the version trap: a model saved under scikit-learn 1.3 and
  loaded under 1.5 may not behave the same. Pin versions in `requirements.txt`
- Deployment of models using Streamlit — ➕ the anatomy of a Streamlit app: widgets in,
  prediction out, `st.cache_resource` so the model loads once
- Offline deployment — batch scoring, scheduled jobs, running locally or on-premise;
  when a CSV of predictions is the right product
- Online deployment — a live app or an API answering one request at a time; ➕ latency,
  concurrency and cost
- ➕ Publishing to Streamlit Community Cloud: repository layout, `requirements.txt`,
  secrets that must not be committed
- ➕ REST APIs as the alternative, with FastAPI in concept — when a UI is the wrong
  interface
- ➕ After deployment: input validation, logging predictions, and **model drift** — the
  world changing under a model that has not
- ➕ Adding a generative-AI layer: an LLM turning the model's numeric output into a
  plain-language explanation for the end user, and the honesty constraint that the
  explanation must not overstate the model

**Demo** — Saving the trained regression model with `joblib`, writing a short Streamlit
script with sliders for the inputs, running it locally, and pushing it to Streamlit
Community Cloud. Then the failure demo: the app deployed without its scaler,
predicting confidently and wrongly.

**Lab** — Deploy the Session 10 loan classifier as a Streamlit app that takes applicant
details, returns an approval probability, and shows the two factors that pushed the
decision most. Publish it and share the link.

**Dataset** — The pipeline saved in Session 10.

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Save the pipeline, not the model"}
A model saved without its scaler and encoder will accept raw input and return a
confident, meaningless number. Nothing raises an error. **`joblib.dump(pipeline, ...)`
— never `joblib.dump(model, ...)`.**
:::

**By the end** — The student can save a full pipeline, build a Streamlit interface for
it, publish it publicly, and name two things that can break it after launch.

### Session 14 — Big Data Analytics: Fundamentals and Distributed Processing {#sec-s14}

*Merges draft Sessions 13 and 14. The fundamentals and the tools that implement them
were separated in the draft with no gain.*

**Topics**

*Fundamentals*

- Working of big data analytics — ➕ the five Vs (volume, velocity, variety, veracity,
  value), and **the honest threshold: the point where one machine stops being enough**
- Types of big data analytics — descriptive, diagnostic, predictive and prescriptive,
  with an example of each
- ➕ Batch versus stream processing, and the architectures that combine them
- Big data analytics technologies and tools — the ecosystem map: HDFS, YARN, Hive,
  HBase, Kafka, Spark, and where each one sits
- ➕ When **not** to use big data tools: a Spark job on 50,000 rows is slower than
  Pandas, and this is measured in the lab

*Distributed storage and processing*

- Apache Hadoop and HDFS — blocks, replication, NameNode and DataNodes, write-once
  semantics
- Big data analytics using MapReduce — map, shuffle, sort, reduce; ➕ word count
  traced by hand on three sentences before any code is run
- ➕ Why MapReduce was replaced: every stage writes to disk
- Implementing big data analytics using Apache Spark — ➕ RDDs and DataFrames, lazy
  evaluation, transformations versus actions, the DAG, in-memory caching
- ➕ Spark SQL and the DataFrame API, which is deliberately close to Pandas
- ➕ PySpark MLlib in brief: the same fit/predict shape, distributed

**Demo** — Exploring HDFS from the terminal with `hdfs dfs -put`, `-get` and `-ls`,
showing how a file is split and replicated across a distributed architecture. Then a
PySpark job performing parallel filtering, grouping and counting over a large mock log
file, timed against the same operation in Pandas.

::: {.callout-important title="🔓 How to run this session on a laptop"}
The draft's HDFS demo assumes a cluster. Three supported paths, in order of
preference:

1. **Docker** — a single-node Hadoop image, so `hdfs dfs` commands are real
2. **PySpark in local mode** — `pip install pyspark`, needs only Java 17; sufficient
   for everything except the HDFS commands themselves
3. **A hosted sandbox or Databricks Community Edition** — no local install

Every code cell in this session runs on path 2. Path 1 is required only for the HDFS
command demo.
:::

**Lab** — Run the same aggregation three times over the mock log file — Pandas, PySpark
local, PySpark with more partitions — and record the wall-clock time for each at 10⁴,
10⁶ and 10⁷ rows. Plot the three curves and identify the crossover point.

**Dataset** — A synthetic web-server log generated by a committed, seeded script,
`datasets/make_logs.py`, at three sizes so the crossover is visible.

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Distributed is not automatically faster"}
Below the crossover, Spark loses to Pandas — the cluster overhead exceeds the work.
Students are expected to find that crossover themselves and quote it, rather than
assert that Spark is fast.
:::

**By the end** — The student can explain HDFS replication, trace a MapReduce word
count by hand, write a PySpark aggregation, and state the row count at which Spark
started to win on their own machine.

### Session 15 — NoSQL Data Stores and Visual Analytics at Scale {#sec-s15}

*Was draft Session 15. "Statistical methods for visualization" is now taught in
[Session 5](#sec-s05) and applied here at scale.*

**Topics**

*NoSQL*

- ➕ Why NoSQL exists: what a relational schema costs when the data is semi-structured
  and the volume is large
- ➕ The four families — document, column-family, key-value, graph — with one use case
  each
- ➕ The CAP theorem in plain language, and eventual consistency as a business decision
  rather than a technical one
- Big data analytics using **MongoDB** — documents and collections, CRUD, indexes, and
  the aggregation pipeline (`$match`, `$group`, `$sort`, `$project`)
- ➕ `pymongo`, and moving results from an aggregation into a Pandas DataFrame
- Big data analytics using **Apache Cassandra** — the wide-column model, partition and
  clustering keys, CQL, and **query-first schema design**, which is the opposite of
  relational normalisation
- ➕ Choosing between them: a comparison table over consistency, write throughput,
  query flexibility and operational cost

*Visualization at scale*

- Statistical methods for visualization, applied to volume — ➕ why a scatter plot of
  ten million points is a solid rectangle
- ➕ Aggregate before you plot: server-side aggregation in the database, then plot the
  summary
- ➕ Sampling for visualization, and the confidence interval that must accompany a
  sampled chart
- ➕ Binning and density: 2-D histograms, hexbin, and datashader-style rasterisation
- ➕ Building a dashboard on aggregated data rather than raw rows

**Demo** — Connecting a Python script to a local MongoDB instance with `pymongo`,
inserting JSON document data, running an aggregate query, and pulling the results back
into Python for visualization. Then the scale demo: the same chart drawn from ten
million raw points and from a database-side aggregation, side by side.

**Lab** — Load the Session 14 log file into MongoDB, write an aggregation pipeline that
answers three questions about traffic by hour and status code, and build a small
dashboard on the aggregated output. Then model the same data for Cassandra and explain
what changes.

**Dataset** — The log file from Session 14, plus
[`loan_data_10k.csv`](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/blob/main/datasets/loan_data_10k.csv)
as documents. **Environment:** MongoDB Community locally, or MongoDB Atlas free tier;
Cassandra via Docker or as a modelling exercise on paper if Docker is unavailable.

**By the end** — The student can write a MongoDB aggregation pipeline, design a
Cassandra table from a query, and produce an honest chart from ten million rows.

### Session 16 — Capstone: The End-to-End Data Science Project {#sec-s16}

*Was draft Session 16, the open-ended module. Now a specified project with a
timetable, deliverables and a marking scheme.*

**Topics and requirements**

- Apply the entire data analytics process to a real-world dataset — collection,
  integration, cleaning, transformation, reduction, EDA, modelling, evaluation,
  deployment
- Perform clustering and association rule mining on a market basket dataset —
  segmenting customers, then explaining each segment with the rules that characterise
  it
- Create insightful visualizations and perform statistical analysis using advanced
  tools — every claim in the report supported by a chart **and** a statistical test
- Develop and implement advanced machine learning models on a complex dataset —
  ensembles, tuned, compared against a stated baseline
- ➕ Project framing: writing a problem statement with a measurable success criterion
  agreed before any modelling starts
- ➕ Reproducibility: seeded, version-pinned, and runnable from a clean clone by
  someone else
- ➕ Responsible data science: the bias audit, the privacy review, the statement of who
  could be harmed by a wrong prediction and how
- ➕ Communicating results: the eight-minute presentation, and reporting what did not
  work

::: {.callout-note title="➕ Deliverables"}
| # | Deliverable | Due |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Problem statement, dataset chosen, success criterion | after Session 5 |
| 2 | EDA report and cleaning log | after Session 8 |
| 3 | Baseline model and evaluation, cross-validated | after Session 11 |
| 4 | Tuned model, deployed app, public link | after Session 13 |
| 5 | Repository, written report, presentation | Session 16 |

The repository must run from a clean clone: `requirements.txt`, a seeded pipeline, and
a README that names the dataset, its licence and its date of retrieval.
:::

**Dataset** — Student's choice from the
[course catalog](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/tree/main/datasets) or an
approved external source, subject to one rule: **it must contain the problem the
project claims to solve.** A clean dataset cannot demonstrate a cleaning pipeline, and
a balanced one cannot demonstrate why accuracy is the wrong metric.

::: {.callout-tip title="✅ A capstone that passes"}
- Runs from a clean clone, first try
- States a success criterion that was fixed before the modelling started
- Beats a named baseline, with the baseline's score printed
- Reports at least one thing that was tried and did not work
- Has a deployed link that a stranger can open
- Says who the model could harm and what was done about it
:::

**By the end** — The student can deliver and defend a complete data science project.

# Course conventions {#sec-conventions}

*These hold in every session. Breaking one in a single session makes every other
session look wrong.*

| Convention | The course does this | Not this |
|---|---|---|
| Environment | one conda environment, **`ds`**, in every session | a per-session environment |
| Split naming | `X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test` | `xtr`, `train_x`, `X1` |
| Categorical encoding | `LabelEncoder` for the target, one-hot for nominal features, printing `le.classes_` | mixing `get_dummies`, `.map({...})` and encoders session by session |
| Preprocessing order | the nine steps of [Part C](#sec-part-c), taught once and referenced afterwards | a different order each session |
| Reproducibility | `random_state` set explicitly, everywhere | unseeded results that change between runs |
| Dataset paths | one `dataset_url`, or one path relative to the project root | a base constant plus a fragment |
| Claims | measured and printed by the code that makes them | asserted in prose |

::: {.callout-important title="🔓 Measure, do not assert"}
Before a session states that a technique helps, the technique is run and the number is
printed. Results from earlier runs of this material that contradicted the textbook
version of the lesson, and were kept:

- Hand-engineered features moved linear R² by **+0.0001** and made the random forest
  **worse**
- The silhouette score **preferred the wrong clustering**
- The "underfitting" decision tree had the **best** test accuracy — because it split on
  a leaked column

**An honest negative result teaches more than a tidy positive one**, because it is what
the student will meet in their own project.
:::

## Tools and environment {#sec-environment}

| Layer | What | Sessions |
|---|---|---|
| Language | Python 3.11 | all |
| Environment | conda environment named `ds`; Google Colab as the no-install fallback | all |
| Core | NumPy, Pandas | 2 onwards |
| Charts | Matplotlib, Seaborn | 5 onwards |
| Statistics | SciPy, statsmodels | 4, 9, 11 |
| Modelling | scikit-learn | 7 onwards |
| Rules | mlxtend | 12 |
| Deployment | Streamlit, joblib | 13 |
| Distributed | PySpark (local mode), Java 17; Hadoop via Docker | 14 |
| Stores | MongoDB Community or Atlas free tier, `pymongo`; Cassandra via Docker | 15 |
| Version control | Git and GitHub | 13, 16 |

```bash
conda create -n ds python=3.11 -y && conda activate ds && pip install -r requirements.txt
```

Every import used anywhere in the course belongs in `requirements.txt`, with versions
pinned — a model saved under one version of scikit-learn and loaded under another is a
[Session 13](#sec-s13) failure mode.

Datasets are reused across sessions on purpose: data the student already knows costs
no explanation, and a course that keeps returning to the same file becomes cumulative.
Every dataset below is chosen because it *contains* the problem its session teaches.

| `regression/salary_data.csv` | one feature, one line | 9 |

Files without a generator script come from the
[course dataset catalog](https://github.com/tech4alltraining/aiml/tree/main/datasets).
Generated files ship with their seeded script committed next to them, so the

## Assessment {#sec-assessment}

➕ Added — the draft did not specify assessment. Weights are a starting point for the
institution to adapt.

| Component | Weight | What is marked |
|---|---|---|
| Session labs (16) | 30% | completed, runs, conclusion stated |
| Assignment 1 — data preparation (after Session 8) | 15% | the cleaning log and the leakage check |
| Assignment 2 — modelling and evaluation (after Session 11) | 15% | metric choice justified; baseline beaten |
| Capstone project | 30% | the five deliverables in [Session 16](#sec-s16) |
| Presentation and viva | 10% | can defend a choice under questioning |

**One rule across all components:** a result that is reported must be reproducible from
the submitted code. A number in a report that the code does not produce is marked as
absent.

# Appendix A — Review of the draft syllabus {#sec-review}

*What the analysis found, and what was done about it. Structural faults first.*

### A.1 Ordering faults — a result that runs and is wrong

**Cleaning before statistics.** The draft detected and removed outliers in Session 3
and taught the interquartile range and standard deviation in Session 7. A student
following the draft removes outliers with a rule they meet four sessions later.
*Fixed:* statistics and EDA are now Sessions 4–5, cleaning is Session 6.

**Scaling before splitting.** The draft applied `MinMaxScaler` and `StandardScaler` in
Session 5 and first mentioned a train–test split in Session 9. Scaling on the full
dataset leaks test-set information into training — the most common serious error in
student projects, and the draft taught it as the default. *Fixed:* the split is taught
in Session 7, immediately before scaling, with leakage as a named topic and `Pipeline`
as the structural remedy.

**PCA before standardisation and before variance.** Session 6 ran PCA; standardisation
was in Session 5 but never connected to it, and variance and correlation were in
Sessions 7–8, after. *Fixed:* reduction is now Session 8, after both.

**Evaluation after everything it should have informed.** Session 11 taught evaluation
after regression (9) and clustering (10), so both were taught with no vocabulary for
judging them. *Fixed:* metrics are taught inline with each model family, and Session 11
— validation strategy, cross-validation, tuning, diagnostics — sits between supervised
learning and clustering.

### A.2 Missing prerequisites

**No Python, no NumPy.** Session 2 opened with Pandas DataFrames. *Fixed:* Session 2 is
now Python and NumPy, with three self-paced pre-work notebooks for students starting
from zero.

**No encoding, no split, no leakage.** No session converted categorical text to
numbers, yet Session 9 trained a regression on real data. *Fixed:* all three are
Session 7.

### A.3 Promised but never taught

| Promised in | Never taught in the draft | Now taught in |
|---|---|---|
| Session 16 — "advanced machine learning models" | classification of any kind | [Session 10](#sec-s10) |
| Session 16 — "association rule mining" | support, confidence, lift, Apriori | [Session 12](#sec-s12) |
| Session 16 — "statistical analysis using advanced tools" | any inferential statistics | [Session 4](#sec-s04) |
| Session 8 demo — "a seaborn correlation heatmap" | Seaborn | [Session 5](#sec-s05) |
| Session 11 — "model evaluation techniques" | cross-validation, over/underfitting | [Session 11](#sec-s11) |

### A.4 Sessions that were the wrong size

**Session 4, Data Integration**, was a five-item taxonomy plus one `.merge()` demo, and
the demo did not illustrate the taxonomy. *Fixed:* merged into Session 3, where the
taxonomy is taught as concepts and the joining is taught as the Pandas skill it is.

**Session 5, Data Transformation**, listed rescaling, normalizing, binarizing and
standardizing — three of which are the same family, and one of which (`Normalizer`)
operates on rows rather than columns, a distinction the draft's phrasing hides. *Fixed:*
the distinction is now an explicit topic, and the session was given the encoding and
splitting content it needed to be a full session.

**Session 9** carried all of supervised learning, including "prediction and decision
making", but demonstrated regression only. *Fixed:* split into Sessions 9 and 10.

### A.5 Terms used without definition

"Data cube aggregation", "numerosity reduction", "top-down discretization" and
"bottom-up discretization" are data-warehousing terms that appear in the draft with no
plain-language definition. They are retained — they are legitimate syllabus content —
and each now has a one-line definition and a Pandas equivalent in
[Session 8](#sec-s08), so the student meets the idea and the tool together.

### A.6 Demos that could not be run

The Session 13 demo explored HDFS through terminal commands, which needs a Hadoop
cluster. The draft gave no execution path. *Fixed:* [Session 14](#sec-s14) names three
supported paths, and every code cell in the session runs on the laptop-only path.

### A.7 What was deliberately kept

- **The 16-session structure**, on the assumption that it is fixed by the schedule
- **Every topic**, including the data-warehousing taxonomy in Session 6 of the draft
  and the five integration approaches in Session 4
- **Every demo**, several extended with a counter-demo showing the same technique
  failing
- **The big-data block**, which several data science syllabi drop; it is consolidated,
  not reduced
